AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: The aim of this study was to examine relationships between work organization features of work hours, work schedules, and job stress with body mass indexes (BMIs) of long-haul truck drivers.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: Face-to-face survey data were collected first, followed by collection of anthropometric measures including height and weight (n = 260). Logistic regression (backward stepwise model) was used to identify significant predictors of BMI and to analyze odds ratios.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Mean BMI was 33.40 kg/m, with 64.2% obese (BMI > 30 kg/m) and 18.4% extreme/morbidly obese (BMI > 40 kg/m). Working more than 11 daily hours was associated with statistically significant increased odds for being extreme obese.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: Findings suggest that longer work hours (>11 hours daily) have a major influence on odds for obesity among this population. The results align with recent NIOSH calls for integrated approaches to worker health.

Article.ArticleTitle: The Work Organization of Long-Haul Truck Drivers and the Association With Body Mass Index.
